note: The player-select roster. Only `record` is measured — it is a real count of hits over attempts from a published study, or the string "unpublished", which is itself the finding for three of the eight. `confidence` and `updates` are 0–5 EDITORIAL JUDGEMENTS, not measurements, and the screen says so in as many words next to the bars. No two records measure the same thing, which is stated on the card.
source: Economist: An, Jalles & Loungani, IMF WP/18/39 (2018) — 5 of 153 recessions called by the consensus in the April before. Perma-bear: 27 bear markets in the 96 years 1928–2024 (Ned Davis Research), i.e. the score for saying it every year. Dartboard and stock picker: the Wall Street Journal's Investment Dartboard, 142 contests 1988–2002 — the darts beat the pros in 55, the pros beat the Dow itself in 76. Superforecaster: Philip Tetlock and Barbara Mellers, IARPA's ACE tournament / the Good Judgment Project, 2011–2015 — the top performers beat the control group by wide margins and outperformed intelligence analysts with access to classified reporting. Octopus Paul: Sea Life Oberhausen — 4 of 6 at Euro 2008 and 8 of 8 at the 2010 World Cup.
statNote: Only the record is measured. Confidence and Updates are our read of how each one behaves, not a number anybody has counted.

characters.name: The Economist
characters.measures: Recessions the forecasting consensus called a year ahead, 1992–2014
characters.line: Competent, careful, and almost never early. The number is low because the question is close to impossible, not because they are bad at their job.

characters.name: The Doomer
characters.measures: Years since 1928 that actually contained a 20% fall — the score for shouting it every January
characters.line: Beats the economists nine times over and has never opened a spreadsheet. He isn't forecasting, he's collecting the base rate and taking the credit.

characters.name: The Pundit
characters.measures: No published record. Nobody is keeping score, which is rather the point.
characters.line: The most confident voice in the piece and the only one with nothing to check. Being unfalsifiable is not a bug in this job, it's the business model.

characters.name: The Algorithm
characters.measures: No published record for calling crashes. Plenty of published backtests, which is not the same thing.
characters.line: Superb at describing what already happened. A backtest is a memory, not a forecast, and the market is the one system that changes because you looked at it.

characters.name: The Dartboard
characters.measures: Rounds the Wall Street Journal's darts beat professional stock pickers, 1988–2002
characters.line: Burton Malkiel said a blindfolded monkey would do about as well as the experts. The Journal spent fourteen years checking. The monkey lost — but not by much.

characters.name: The Stock Picker
characters.tag: Beat the darts, not the market
characters.measures: Rounds those same professionals beat the Dow itself
characters.line: Won the contest against a dartboard, then went 76–66 against the index. That is a coin flip, and a coin flip doesn't charge a management fee.

characters.name: The Superforecaster
characters.measures: Scored on probability accuracy over thousands of questions, not on hits — the top performers beat analysts with classified intelligence
characters.line: Never says a crash is coming. Says 15 percent, then 12, then 20, and tells you why it moved. The only one here who has been properly scored and came out well — and the least fun to listen to.

characters.name: Octopus Paul
characters.measures: Football matches called by walking into one of two boxes of mussels
characters.line: Eight from eight at the 2010 World Cup — a 1-in-256 run. He never explained himself, never revised a target, and died undefeated in October 2010. No human on this screen managed the second one.
